controls.detail: Because SAM and GSAM require roughly twice the computation per step, vanilla training is run for twice their number of epochs.
controls.rules_out: That GSAM's gains are explained merely by giving it more training computation or training time.

confounds.name: Longer training, rather than the GSAM intervention, explains the gains
confounds.detail: SAM and GSAM require roughly twice the computation per step, so their gains could reflect unequal training compute.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper runs vanilla training for twice the epochs and reports no significant improvement from the longer training.

confounds.name: A smaller surrogate gap may not indicate a smaller actual dominant Hessian eigenvalue
confounds.detail: The claimed sharpness improvement could be an artifact of using the surrogate gap as a proxy.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper compares σ_max≈2h/ρ² with dominant eigenvalues calculated by power iteration on a training-set subset; the trends match.

evidence_standards.name: Standard deviation is not reported in the main comparison
evidence_standards.detail: The paper says it ignores standard deviation because it is typically negligible (<0.1%) compared with the reported improvements; it does not specify seeds, a statistical test, or confidence intervals.

metrics.name: Test accuracy
metrics.caveat: Confirms generalization but does not reveal how the model solves the task; the paper also reports top-five-frequency spectral ablation accuracy and Fraction of Variance Explained (FVE).

controls.name: LayerNorm and RMSNorm reference models
controls.detail: Standard-normalization models provide comparisons alongside the spherical configurations, including with learned attention.
controls.rules_out: Shows whether the reported dynamics differ from the paper’s standard-normalization reference conditions.

controls.name: LayerNorm with normalized unembedding
controls.detail: The LayerNorm baseline is given an L₂-normalized unembedding, while retaining internal residual magnitude freedom.
controls.rules_out: Rules out normalized unembedding or bounded output logits alone as sufficient to eliminate delayed generalization.

controls.name: S₅ negative-control task
controls.detail: The spherical topology is evaluated on non-commutative S₅ composition alongside LayerNorm and RMSNorm baselines; spherical models fail to generalize within the training window while baselines succeed on most seeds.
controls.rules_out: A differential outcome argues against the spherical constraint being a generic optimization accelerator, and supports task-specific alignment.

controls.name: Learned-attention comparison for uniform attention
controls.detail: Uniform-attention configurations are compared with learned-attention configurations on the same tasks; on S₅, uniform-attention baselines reach about 99% peak accuracy without meaningful acceleration relative to learned attention.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether removing data-dependent routing is sufficient for the observed behavior, and whether routing is the primary bottleneck on the non-commutative task.

controls.name: L₁-normalized topology on S₅
controls.detail: The paper additionally evaluates L₁ normalization, which imposes cross-polytope geometry, and reports that it also fails to generalize on S₅.
controls.rules_out: Shows that the reported S₅ failure is not unique to the tested L₂ spherical constraint among the simple norm-based topologies examined.

confounds.name: The spherical constraint is a generic optimizer stabilizer rather than a task-aligned bias
confounds.detail: If it were a generic stabilizer, it should also reduce delayed generalization on the non-commutative S₅ task.
confounds.ruled_out_by: On S₅, spherical models reach perfect training accuracy but fail to generalize on all seeds within 100,000 epochs, while LayerNorm and RMSNorm baselines generalize on most seeds.

confounds.name: The effect comes from bounded output logits rather than constraining the residual stream
confounds.detail: An L₂-normalized unembedding could itself limit logit growth and account for the apparent improvement.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The LayerNorm baseline with normalized unembedding still exhibits a prolonged memorization phase.

confounds.name: High test accuracy comes from a shortcut rather than the Fourier circuit
confounds.detail: Accuracy alone does not identify the representation or mechanism used to solve the task.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper performs top-five-frequency spectral ablations, which preserve over 99% accuracy in successful configurations, and measures FVE of the expected sine/cosine basis.

confounds.name: A learned solution may memorize rather than generalize
confounds.detail: With insufficient data, feature learning can converge to non-generalizable memorization solutions, so training progress or energy alone would not establish generalization.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Report test accuracy and inspect whether the learned solutions are generalizable Fourier-basis solutions or non-generalizable solutions such as memorization.

controls.name: AdamW-srf
controls.detail: Compared with HomeAdamW; uses the square-root-free AdamW update without HomeAdamW's threshold-based switch to momentum-based SGD.
controls.rules_out: A difference isolates the effect of HomeAdamW's conditional switch from the square-root-free AdamW update.

datasets.name: FineWeb-Edu
datasets.eval_protocol: Pre-train GPT-style decoder-only Transformers with AdamW for 10,000 steps using a Warmup-Stable-Decay schedule (20% warmup, 60% stable, 20% decay), batch size 1024 (about 1M tokens per step); sweep peak learning rate and weight decay across widths 128–2048, increasing the number of heads while fixing head dimension at 64. Also evaluate a compute-optimal setting at 20 tokens per parameter. The paper analyzes training loss across learning rates and widths; it does not specify a dataset split.

datasets.name: CIFAR-100
datasets.eval_protocol: Train CNNs to compare transfer with an SP input-layer learning rate of Θ(1) and with a change to last-layer initialization; split, trial count, and scoring details are not specified.

baselines.name: Standard Parameterization (SP)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with μP using GPT-style Transformers, the same training setup and width sweep, and peak learning-rate and weight-decay sweeps.

baselines.name: Maximal Update Parameterization (μP)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with SP using GPT-style Transformers, the same training setup and width sweep, and peak learning-rate and weight-decay sweeps.

metrics.name: Loss Predictability Error (𝓔)
metrics.caveat: Measures how well the loss landscape fits the paper’s scaling ansatz, but does not measure sensitivity to learning-rate extrapolation errors or asymptotic performance; the paper reports transfer robustness exponent κ and asymptotic loss degradation 𝓡(∞) alongside it.

metrics.name: Transfer Robustness Exponent (κ)
metrics.caveat: Measures whether the normalized loss landscape flattens or sharpens with width, but does not establish loss predictability or performance at scale; the paper reports 𝓔 and 𝓡(∞) alongside it.

metrics.name: Asymptotic Loss Degradation (𝓡(∞))
metrics.caveat: Measures the asymptotic loss gap relative to the best parameterization considered, but does not measure fit quality or robustness to extrapolation errors; the paper reports 𝓔 and κ alongside it.

controls.name: SP with Θ(1) embedding learning rate (SP+Embd)
controls.detail: Change SP’s embedding learning rate from Θ(1/n) to Θ(1), leaving the other SP changes out.
controls.rules_out: That μP’s transfer advantage requires its full set of parameterization changes; this condition essentially matches μP across the three transfer metrics.

controls.name: μP with Θ(1/n) embedding learning rate (μP-Embd)
controls.detail: Reduce μP’s embedding learning rate from Θ(1) to Θ(1/n).
controls.rules_out: That fast embedding learning is incidental to μP’s advantage; transfer quality degrades when this feature is removed.

controls.name: Attention-scaling ablations (SP+Attn and μP-Attn)
controls.detail: Add μP’s 1/d attention scaling to SP, or remove it from μP.
controls.rules_out: That the embedding-layer result is explained by attention scaling alone; these ablations instead make κ strongly positive.

controls.name: LayerNorm-learning-rate ablations (SP+LN and μP-LN)
controls.detail: Raise SP’s LayerNorm learning rate to Θ(1), or lower μP’s to Θ(1/n).
controls.rules_out: That changing the LayerNorm learning rate accounts for μP’s advantage; raising it in SP worsens instability, while lowering it in μP has negligible effect.

controls.name: μP with SP-like last-layer initialization (μP-Last)
controls.detail: Change μP’s last-layer initialization variance to Θ(1/n).
controls.rules_out: That the last-layer initialization change is the primary driver of μP’s transfer advantage; its effect is reported as negligible overall, though instability appears at small widths.

controls.name: Frozen embedding layer
controls.detail: Freeze the embedding layer at initialization in both SP and μP.
controls.rules_out: That later layers can fully compensate for an untrained embedding; freezing hurts both parameterizations, especially μP.

controls.name: Weight-decay comparisons, including λ=0
controls.detail: Compare parameterizations across weight-decay strengths, including no weight decay.
controls.rules_out: That weight decay alone explains stability or transfer: stable SP+Embd and μP results occur without it, and weight decay does not fully stabilize SP and SP+LN.

confounds.name: The apparent benefit could be due to last-layer initialization rather than embedding learning rate
confounds.detail: μP changes both the embedding learning rate and last-layer initialization; the latter could otherwise account for differences in stability or transfer.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Ablate last-layer initialization (including μP-Last) and compare the transfer metrics; the paper finds its effect negligible overall, unlike the embedding-learning-rate change.

confounds.name: Later layers might compensate for a slowly trained or untrained embedding
confounds.detail: If later layers could learn around an inadequate embedding, the embedding learning rate need not be the cause of the observed performance and stability differences.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Switch embedding learning rates during training and freeze the embedding at initialization; slowing it causes persistent loss gaps, and freezing it hurts both parameterizations, especially μP.

confounds.name: The embedding-layer effect might be specific to Transformers
confounds.detail: If the effect depended on Transformer-specific structure, it would not support the broader claim that the input layer is especially important.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Test CNNs on CIFAR-100: SP with a Θ(1) input-layer learning rate matches μP’s transfer quality, while changing only last-layer initialization has little effect.

confounds.name: Weight decay, rather than embedding learning rate, could explain improved stability or predictability
confounds.detail: Weight decay can regularize the loss landscape and reduce predictability error, potentially making it appear that the embedding intervention is responsible.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Sweep weight decay and compare with λ=0; stable parameterizations perform well without weight decay, while weight decay alone is insufficient to match them or stabilize SP+LN.

evidence_standards.name: One random seed per configuration
evidence_standards.detail: The authors state that each configuration is run with a single random seed because of the large hyperparameter sweep. No statistical test, variance estimate, confidence interval, or numerical margin for declaring a difference real is specified.

baselines.name: standard parameterization
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared in the same parameterization ablation; for the learning-rate-transfer comparison, models are trained to 10 tokens per parameter and the number of KV-head repetitions is varied. For the learning-rate/weight-decay sweep, the initial standard deviation is held constant.

baselines.name: vanilla Adam-μP
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared in the same parameterization ablation; for the learning-rate-transfer comparison, models are trained to 10 tokens per parameter and the number of KV-head repetitions is varied. For the learning-rate/weight-decay sweep, the initial standard deviation is held constant, with hidden dimension, depth, batch size, and training iterations scaled.

metrics.name: optimal learning rate
metrics.caveat: GQA training becomes noisier as the number of KV heads decreases; the paper reports the mean and standard deviation across optimal learning rates.

metrics.name: optimal weight decay
metrics.caveat: Transfer is assessed across model sizes; the paper reports variance across sizes rather than relying only on the plotted loss landscapes.

metrics.name: τ_epoch
metrics.caveat: Prior work argues this quantity, rather than weight decay, should transfer; the paper measures both and reports their variance across model sizes.

metrics.name: activation update norm ||Δhᶩₜ||₂
metrics.caveat: Can misleadingly indicate feature learning and learning-rate transfer even when weight updates fail the spectral coordinate check; the paper also measures weight-update norms.

metrics.name: weight-update spectral norm ||ΔW||
metrics.caveat: For rank-degenerate GQA weights, the spectral norm can misrepresent deformation on typical inputs; the paper introduces and analyzes the expected operator norm for this setting.

metrics.name: expected operator norm
metrics.caveat: Defined relative to the input distribution; the paper uses Gaussian i.i.d. inputs and motivates it because the spectral norm can misrepresent low-rank GQA behavior.

controls.name: vanilla Adam-μP scaling
controls.detail: Ablation that uses the vanilla Adam-μP implementation, treating KV heads as hidden layers rather than applying the proposed GQA-specific scaling.
controls.rules_out: A difference from GQA-μP supports the claim that the GQA-specific scaling, rather than merely using μP, enables the reported transfer behavior.

confounds.name: activation coordinate checks can appear to show feature learning without correctly scaled weight updates
confounds.detail: Changes in activations can arise from both weight updates and changing inputs, so activation-update norms may suggest transferable dynamics even when the weight updates are incorrectly scaled.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Measure weight-update spectral norms directly: the vanilla implementation fails this coordinate check while the proposed GQA scaling passes.

confounds.name: apparent weight-decay transfer may instead be transfer of τ_epoch
confounds.detail: A result attributed to weight decay could be explained by the alternative claim that τ_epoch, not weight decay, is the transferable quantity.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Measure and compare the across-model-size variances of learning rate, weight decay, and τ_epoch; the paper reports that both weight decay and τ_epoch transfer in its setting.

evidence_standards.name: Reported variability for transfer comparisons
evidence_standards.detail: Figure 1 reports mean optimal learning rates with standard-deviation shading; the weight-decay and τ_epoch analyses report variances across model sizes. The paper does not specify a statistical test, confidence interval, or threshold for declaring a difference real.

evidence_standards.name: 1000 independent draws for the norm demonstration
evidence_standards.detail: Figure 2 averages each point over 1000 independent draws and shows a band of ±1 standard deviation.

metrics.name: Generalization (population/test) squared loss
metrics.caveat: In regression it typically decays smoothly without an explicit test-error plateau; the paper also reports a threshold-based surrogate accuracy to reveal plateauing.

metrics.name: Threshold-based surrogate accuracy
metrics.caveat: Defined as the probability that squared prediction error is at most ε; used because continuous regression loss typically has no explicit plateau.

evidence_standards.name: 50 independent runs for Figure 1
evidence_standards.detail: Runs use independent datasets and student initializations; no statistical test, variance estimate, or threshold for declaring a difference is stated.

confounds.name: The reproduced optimizer ranking could be an artifact of selecting trials by training loss rather than validation performance
confounds.detail: Wilson et al. selected trials by training loss and then reported test results, which could explain a ranking difference without the paper’s tuning-protocol explanation being correct.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper instead selects using validation performance and reports test performance; it says this change does not alter the result.

confounds.name: The selected hyperparameter optima could lie at search-space boundaries
confounds.detail: If optima were boundary-limited, the reported comparisons could reflect an inadequate search space rather than optimizer performance under tuning.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper reports checking that optimal hyperparameter values were away from search-space boundaries in all experiments.

confounds.name: Optimizer rankings could depend on the chosen step budgets or target errors
confounds.detail: The headline comparisons, especially training-speed rankings, might result from the particular budgets or target errors chosen.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper reports that the inclusion-consistent results also hold under alternative step budgets and error targets in Appendix E.

confounds.name: Batch size could change the gaps between optimizers
confounds.detail: The paper notes prior empirical work showing that increasing batch size can increase training-time gaps, so the reported comparisons may not hold at other batch sizes.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out: the paper says it did not measure the effects of varying batch size.

confounds.name: The findings may depend on the workloads and tuning protocol considered
confounds.detail: Different workloads, search spaces, trial budgets, or learning-rate schedule parameterizations could produce different optimizer comparisons.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out generally: the paper limits its detailed findings to similar workloads and protocols, while reporting comparisons across its evaluated workloads.

evidence_standards.name: 10, 50, or 100 feasible tuning trials per workload; bootstrap-estimated means and uncertainties
evidence_standards.detail: The paper uses quasi-random uniform search, continuing until it obtains the fixed number of feasible trials. It describes inclusion-consistent comparisons as holding within error bars; it does not specify a formal statistical test or a numerical margin for declaring a tie.

metrics.name: training accuracy
metrics.caveat: High training accuracy does not establish performance on client validation data; the paper reports validation/testing accuracy alongside it.

metrics.name: validation/testing accuracy
metrics.caveat: An aggregate score can conceal differences in performance across clients; the paper also reports best and worst local-client accuracy (the deviation).

metrics.name: communication rounds to target testing accuracy
best and worst local-client accuracy (deviation)
metrics.caveat: Average performance alone can conceal poor performance or large deviations among clients; the paper reports best and worst local accuracy to show this variation.

controls.name: FedAvg unmodified reference
controls.detail: The paper evaluates FedAvg alongside FedSAM and MoFedSAM as the standard non-momentum FL reference.
controls.rules_out: A difference from FedAvg supports an effect beyond simply running ordinary federated ERM training.

controls.name: FedSAM comparison for MoFedSAM
controls.detail: FedSAM is evaluated alongside MoFedSAM; the paper states MoFedSAM with momentum parameter β=1 is equivalent to FedSAM.
controls.rules_out: A difference against FedSAM supports a contribution from MoFedSAM's added momentum mechanism, rather than SAM local optimization alone.

confounds.name: Aggregate accuracy may conceal poor or uneven client performance
confounds.detail: A favorable aggregate result could coexist with poor outcomes for some clients or substantial client-to-client variation, rather than indicating improved generality across clients.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper reports best and worst local-client accuracy and discusses the resulting deviation.

confounds.name: Training performance may reflect overfitting rather than generalization to client validation data
confounds.detail: Training accuracy gains could occur without corresponding performance on validation data, which may have a different distribution from each client's training data.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper reports training and validation/testing accuracy alongside one another.

evidence_standards.name: Average and standard deviation
evidence_standards.detail: The results table reports average (standard deviation) for training and validation accuracy. The excerpt does not specify the number of runs or seeds, a statistical test, or a numerical margin for treating differences as real.

metrics.name: maximum NTK eigenvalue (curvature)

controls.detail: Alongside fixed-step runs, models are evolved for matched physical time t·η; the learning rate is then decayed to the same final learning rate.
controls.rules_out: That the apparent learning-rate advantage is only due to unequal physical training time or, toward the end of training, unequal SGD noise.

confounds.detail: With the same number of steps, a small-learning-rate model can remain close to initialization, making its performance look worse for reasons other than the catapult effect.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Also compares models evolved for the same physical time t·η.

confounds.name: different SGD noise explains the performance difference
confounds.detail: Learning-rate choices can change SGD noise, which could account for the observed generalization differences independently of the proposed curvature-reduction mechanism.
confounds.ruled_out_by: For the CIFAR comparisons, decays the learning rate at a fixed physical time to the same final learning rate, which the paper says ensures the same level of SGD noise toward the end; it also reports a full-batch gradient-descent MNIST experiment.

confounds.name: The association between lower test variance and better generalization may not mean test collapse causes better generalization

The authors note that reduced test variance may be necessary for improved test error because high variance can produce noisy classification decisions.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out: the authors explicitly caution that this experiment is not evidence of a mechanistic relationship.

confounds.name: Finite-time measurements may not represent collapse in the t→∞ limit
confounds.detail: The train-set-size experiment measures collapse at finite training time; the authors note that train variance would be identically zero at t→∞ under the collapse definition, while test variance could still vary with data size.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out: the authors acknowledge this as a limitation of the experiment.

confounds.name: Run-to-run stochasticity could make a single run misleading
confounds.detail: Random mini-batch sampling and initial parameters can change optimizer performance, so an apparent difference might reflect random variation rather than the method.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Run each selected optimizer/problem setting 10 times with different random seeds; the reported table values are averages over the runs.

confounds.name: Training performance may not represent generalization
confounds.detail: Optimizers with similar training performance can have different held-out performance, so a training-only result could give the same apparent headline while concealing poor generalization.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluate held-out test loss and accuracy alongside training loss and accuracy; at test evaluations, also evaluate a larger training chunk as the train-eval set.

confounds.name: A surrogate loss may not reflect the metric users care about
confounds.detail: In classification, optimizers can have similar or differently ranked losses while achieving different accuracies.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Report loss and accuracy together when available; the benchmark uses test accuracy for its performance measure when available, otherwise test loss.

confounds.name: Baselines could appear weaker because they received less hyperparameter-tuning effort
confounds.detail: Unequal attention or tuning could make a new optimizer look better without a genuine method advantage.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Tune each baseline's learning rate separately on every test problem using the same 36-point logarithmic grid from 10^-5 to 10^2, then run the selected setting 10 times.

confounds.name: Results could depend on cherry-picked problems or optimizer overfitting to familiar benchmarks
confounds.detail: Choosing convenient problems, or repeatedly designing around a narrow set of established datasets and architectures, could make results look favorable without broad performance.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Use the fixed DeepOBS problem sets and evaluate across both the small and large benchmark sets, spanning eight different problems.

confounds.detail: The paper observes that Fira can converge faster early, while APOLLO catches up later and appears to benefit from more training tokens; a final comparison could therefore reflect training duration rather than a uniform advantage throughout training.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors plot training-stage validation perplexity and compare LLaMA-130M runs at 20K and 30K steps. These measurements show APOLLO catching up with more tokens, so the paper does not rule out token count as an explanation for some comparisons.

metrics.name: Expected performance after k hyperparameter-search trials
Probability an optimizer outperforms the others on a randomly chosen task at a given budget
metrics.caveat: Does not show the margin by which an optimizer underperforms; the paper also reports aggregated relative performance S(o,k).

metrics.name: Aggregated relative performance S(o,k), relative to the best optimizer on each task at that budget
Quartiles of performance across search outcomes

confounds.name: A fixed number of training epochs could favor an optimizer that reaches good performance earlier
confounds.detail: Optimizers may reach good performance at different rates, so comparing them at a fixed epoch count could bias the result.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Uses validation-set performance for stopping: training stops when validation loss plateaus for more than 2 epochs or the DeepOBS maximum epoch count is reached.

confounds.name: Using random-search trials rather than computation time as the budget could drive the conclusions
confounds.detail: Optimizers may differ in runtime, so a trial-budget comparison might not reflect performance under a time-constrained budget.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Appendix F also evaluates with time as the budget unit and reports that the conclusions remain valid.

confounds.name: Independent hyperparameter priors may miss useful interactions and disadvantage an optimizer
confounds.detail: The paper acknowledges that complex relationships between hyperparameters may exist and that its univariate independent priors do not model them.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Appendix H tests the effective-learning-rate approach and finds it improves lower-budget HPO performance; the authors acknowledge this does not model causal relationships between parameters and do not rule the concern out.

evidence_standards.name: Bootstrap estimates over the empirical hyperparameter library
evidence_standards.detail: Precomputes a library much larger than budget B, resamples B entries to simulate search, and uses bootstrap resampling to estimate performance after a budget. For the mean and variance of the best performance, it uses the closed-form method of Dodge et al. (2019). The paper does not specify a fixed number of repetitions, seeds, statistical test, or significance margin.
